abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for analyzing complex networks through combinatorial rigidity theory, representing a fundamental shift from metric-based approaches to constraint-based network characterization. We establish a formal equivalence between network resilience and matroid structure properties, demonstrating that extremal network behavior can be precisely captured by identifying minimal rigid substructures. This paradigm shift reveals that classical percolation phenomena admit natural combinatorial interpretations via polymatroid functions and submodular optimization. Our primary theoretical contribution establishes tight extremal bounds on critical thresholds for constrained network models, characterized entirely through combinatorial invariants rather than probabilistic parameters. We prove that phase transitions in random network models correspond to changes in the combinatorial depth of associated matroid structures. The framework yields a new research direction connecting discrete mathematics, combinatorial optimization, and network science through the unified lens of combinatorial rigidity. Computational complexity analysis confirms that identifying critical network components remains tractable under our framework, with algorithms running in O(n log n) time for bounded-degree networks. This work opens novel avenues for analyzing infrastructure networks, epidemic spreading processes, and synchronization phenomena through purely combinatorial methods.

We present a significant theoretical improvement to the complexity analysis of parameterized algorithms for the Vertex Cover problem on graphs with bounded treewidth. While existing algorithms achieve O(2^{O(k)}n) time, we develop refined combinatorial techniques that reduce the exponential factor dependence, establishing new upper bounds of O(1.2738^k n) for the general case. Our approach combines iterative compression with an enhanced branch-and-bound strategy based on novel crown decomposition bounds. We prove that the reduction rules can be applied more aggressively when certain connectivity conditions hold, yielding stronger pruning guarantees. The theoretical analysis introduces a new measure of graph structuredness that captures essential algorithmic features more precisely than traditional treewidth-based measures. We also establish matching lower bounds under the strong exponential time hypothesis, demonstrating that further improvements would imply breakthrough results in satisfiability algorithms. The techniques developed extend naturally to related problems including Steiner Tree and Feedback Vertex Set, where we obtain analogous improvements. Experimental evaluation on standard benchmark instances confirms that the refined bounds translate into substantial practical speedups, with running times reduced by factors of 2-5 compared to previous state-of-the-art implementations.

This paper presents GraphFlow, a novel streaming graph processing system designed for continuous analysis of dynamic networks. Unlike batch-oriented frameworks, GraphFlow introduces a window-based computational model that maintains materialized views of network properties with sub-linear update costs. The system architecture employs a hierarchical aggregation design where local neighborhood statistics are maintained incrementally while global properties are recomputed only when significant structural changes occur. We design novel algorithms for maintaining betweenness centrality, PageRank, and clustering coefficients under vertex and edge insertions with worst-case O(1) update complexity for bounded-degree graphs. The system supports a flexible query language enabling complex analytical workloads including temporal pattern matching and dynamic community detection. Extensive evaluation on real-world dynamic networks with millions of edges demonstrates that GraphFlow achieves 10-100x speedups over state-of-the-art systems while maintaining interactive response times for streaming workloads. The proposed window semantics provide formal guarantees on approximation bounds for sliding window queries. This work establishes a new paradigm for graph analytics that naturally accommodates the temporal dimension inherent in modern network data.

We present substantial engineering improvements to branch-and-bound solvers for the quadratic assignment problem, achieving order-of-magnitude performance gains over previous implementations. Our contributions span multiple levels of the solver architecture. At the lower level, we develop cache-aware data structures for maintaining the incumbent solution and partial assignments that reduce memory bandwidth requirements by 60%. The branching strategy incorporates machine learning-based strong branching heuristics trained on instance features, reducing the number of explored nodes by 40% on benchmark instances. We introduce a portfolio-based approach for adaptive selection of local search procedures, dynamically choosing between simulated annealing, tabu search, and variable neighborhood descent based on runtime feedback. The bounding procedure is enhanced with a new eigenvalue-based bound that dominates classical Gilmore-Lawler bounds while maintaining comparable computational overhead. Experimental results on standard QAPLIB instances demonstrate that the improved solver solves instances up to 50% larger within given time limits, with average speedup of 15x over previous state-of-the-art. The system scales effectively to multi-core architectures through fine-grained parallelization of the bounding and branching operations.
